title: At four alpine sites in 2021, seedling presence was 19% below an independent seed success benchmark
abstract: We tested whether average seed success predicts the first-season presence of supplied lower-elevation plant species. We used a Norwegian field experiment with four alpine sites, warming and vegetation gap treatments, 10,900 supplied seeds and 420 species-by-plot units. The 412 final live seedlings occupied 152 units. An exact independent-seed benchmark, conditional on all 84 species, site and treatment totals, expected 186.98 units. Presence was 18.7% below that benchmark. The recorded emergence distribution accounted for 82.1% of this finite-data deficit in a two-stage diagnostic; this is not a causal process share. In 22 folds that excluded recorded blocks, a binomial model predicted 194.49 occupied units and a beta-binomial model predicted 154.49. Both predicted about 412 live seedlings. The beta-binomial improved the presence log score by 0.074 per unit, with an approximate block interval of 0.022 to 0.128. The result remained in the 18 complete blocks and with species-specific treatment slopes. Warming contrasts in final presence were uncertain. The source study already found vegetation and emergence effects. We add a count-to-presence test and withheld prediction evidence for clustered recruitment after seed supply. One season, selected species, four sites, unmatched block labels and unmeasured seed fate limit inference. The result does not identify the physical cause of clustering, adult establishment, or a share of the thermal-tracking gap. Own code, aggregate results, a figure and exact external-data retrieval instructions are included.

display.caption: The same 412 final live seedlings occupied 152 species-by-plot units, versus 187 under independent seed success. Retaining the observed emergence distribution reduces expected final presence to 158.2. A beta-binomial model predicts withheld presence more closely than a binomial model. Physical causes of clustering and later establishment remain unknown.
